Home SOC Lab / Investigation 01

SMB password guessing.
Following the logon trail.

14 November 2026
Analyst: Nicholas Adriel
Personally owned lab · Simulated activity

I wanted to see what Windows and Wazuh would record when a remote client tried incorrect passwords and then a valid one. I ran a controlled SMB password-guessing test and reviewed the resulting authentication evidence. Wazuh displayed three failed-logon alerts followed by a successful network-logon alert.

Target
win-victim2 · Windows 11192.168.13.129 · SMB / TCP 445
Test source
Kali Linux192.168.13.130 · NetExec
Detection source
Windows Security → WazuhSysmon is installed in the lab; its contribution is not demonstrated here.

What I did

  • Confirmed that the lab target exposed SMB on TCP port 445.
  • Used a small password list against the local account Victim.
  • Reviewed the Wazuh event list and the successful Windows Security event.
  • Documented what the screenshots establish and where further checks are needed.

What the result means

The terminal confirms that a valid password authenticated to SMB. Windows recorded a successful network logon, and Wazuh surfaced it alongside earlier failure alerts.

This is a password-guessing exercise (T1110.001). It does not demonstrate remote command execution, file access, or complete host compromise.

Claims and supporting evidence

Observed facts and interpretation limits
ClaimEvidenceLimit
SMB was reachable.The Nmap capture shows 445/tcp open.This proves service exposure at test time, not exploitation.
The password test authenticated successfully.The NetExec capture shows a successful local credential result; the Windows capture shows Event 4624 for Victim.No post-authentication activity is demonstrated.
Wazuh displayed failures before a success.Three 60122 alerts followed by a 92652 alert on the same agent.The failed events are not expanded in the supplied evidence. Matching their account and source IP still needs verification.
The alert label needs analyst validation.Rule 92652 says “possible pass-the-hash”, but the test supplied plaintext password candidates.The label does not establish pass-the-hash. No custom correlation rule is claimed.

Authentication timeline

Dashboard timestamps as displayed · 14 November 2026 · approximate seconds
Displayed timeObservationWazuh rule
11:37:49First visible logon-failure alert60122
11:37:51Second visible logon-failure alert60122
11:37:53Third visible logon-failure alert60122
11:37:55Successful remote logon alert for Victim92652

These are alert-list timestamps, not a reconstructed raw-event timeline. The successful Windows event records 2026-11-14T04:37:53.1183079Z (UTC), equivalent to 11:37:53 WIB. The terminal uses EST. Different clock displays and event-versus-alert timestamps must be normalized before calculating delays or claiming detection latency.

Evidence gallery

Select a screenshot to enlarge it. The captures are preserved as supplied. Unrelated alerts remain visible for context and are excluded from the investigation claims.

Supporting captures: password list and lab dashboard

Detection interpretation

The successful event comes from Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing, channel Security. Logon type 3 means network logon; it is not an interactive desktop session.

The sequence is consistent with the password-guessing test I ran. A production investigation would also require inspecting the failed events’ username, source IP, failure codes, and timestamps before grouping them with the success.

Next validation steps

  • Inspect each failed authentication event and verify the account, source, and failure reason.
  • Build and test a failure-then-success correlation rule.
  • Test stronger passwords, account lockout settings, and restricted SMB firewall access.

These are planned follow-up tests, not completed controls or measured improvements.

Scope: an analyst-run exercise against a personally owned Windows VM. No third-party target, production incident, packet-capture analysis, custom detection rule, or measured remediation result is presented.
